description: Five-Body Problem: five people, many languages, one orbit. We're a Vienna-based team of two students and three experienced professionals. We combine software engineering, data analysis, product thinking and design, and we love turning NASA data into tools people actually use. We work fast, argue kindly and always ship a working demo.
summary: A passport for space cargo: what it is made of, which NASA fire experiments apply where it is going, and what is still untested. For every shipment, Cargo Passport lists the items and their materials, follows the cargo along its route (Earth, ISS, Moon) and compares oxygen, pressure, gravity and airflow at each stop with the conditions of NASA tests: NASA PSI microgravity combustion experiments and NASA-STD-6001 / NTRS material tests. It summarizes the evidence per material, ranks test records by how closely their conditions match the destination (a reading order, not a risk score), and an SI explanation interprets the comparison with a citation for every sentence. Untested conditions stay visible as unknown. Cargo Passport organises evidence for people to review; it is not a safety verdict.
details:
Flames behave differently in microgravity: hot gases do not rise, so oxygen, airflow and materials decide how a fire spreads. NASA has run hundreds of combustion experiments, but each result holds only for the conditions it was tested in. A bag tested on the ISS at 21% O2 tells little about a lunar habitat scenario at 30% O2 and 1/6 g. Today that gap is invisible to the people who pack, ship and store cargo.

Cargo Passport gives every shipment a passport page that a QR code on the crate can open: each cargo item and its materials, compared with NASA test records (NASA PSI microgravity combustion experiments such as BASS, BASS-II, SAFFIRE, FLEX, SAME and ACME, plus NASA-STD-6001 and NTRS material tests); a route view (Earth, ISS, Moon, Mars) that compares oxygen, pressure and gravity at every stop; and an evidence comparison per material that says what matches the target environment, what differs and what is unknown. Where there is no evidence the passport says so. An SI explanation summarises the findings with sources; it does not invent results and gives no emergency instructions. The same method works on Earth wherever cargo moves into new conditions: aircraft holds, submarines, battery storage, schools.

Story site (start here): a guided walk-through of the passport for one illustrative item, with every number linked to a verbatim quote from its NASA source, and short stories on what the PSI experiments show and what is still unknown.

How it answers the challenge: it summarizes (one passport per shipment: materials, route conditions and the NASA test records that apply), ranks (test records ordered by how well their conditions match the destination: exact, related, analogue, then by how many conditions differ or are unknown; a reading order, not a safety score) and interprets (an SI explanation that cites a record for every sentence and keeps untested conditions visible).

How it works: (1) Evidence: NASA PSI microgravity experiments and NASA-STD-6001 / NTRS material tests. (2) Compare: deterministic code compares each test's conditions with every stop of the cargo's journey. (3) SI explains the comparison with sources. (4) People decide: how to ship, where to store, what to test next.

Not a safety verdict: Cargo Passport organises evidence for review and does not approve cargo for flight. The shipment in the video is illustrative. Unknown values stay "unknown" where no source gives them; the 30% O2, about 0.69 atm lunar case is a scenario taken from the challenge brief, and NASA planning documents cite 34% O2 at 8.2 psia for future lunar habitats.

Built with: Python, FastAPI and PostgreSQL (API, Alembic migrations, NASA PSI ingest, comparison logic), a single-file vanilla JavaScript frontend, a static story site, curated NASA data (24 PSI investigation records, NASA-STD-6001, NTRS papers). SI use: Claude Sonnet 5.5 (Anthropic) powers the Explain feature; the code, data-normalisation scripts and docs were written with SI coding assistants (Claude, Codex) and reviewed and tested by the team; Claude Opus checks that each story-site claim says no more than its quote; the video narration is synthetic speech (Kokoro-82M TTS via HyperFrames); every SI-generated image and video frame carries an "SI-assisted" watermark.
